explanation_E: Option E is incorrect because the argument defines the starting point as a planet "capable of supporting life," which is not necessarily restricted to planets exactly "the size of Earth." Thus, the probability of having Earth-sized planets in systems with large planets does not directly address the core relationship between comet threats and the emergence of life.

Explanation:
The stimulus exhibits a classic quantifiers flaw (or quantifier overlap error). The arguer premises that not all tenured faculty are full professors (which means some tenured faculty are not full professors) and that every faculty member in the linguistics department has tenure (which means all linguistics faculty are tenured). From this, the arguer concludes that not all linguistics faculty are full professors (some linguistics faculty are not full professors).

This reasoning is flawed because the subset of tenured faculty who are not full professors does not have to overlap with the linguistics department. All linguistics faculty members could be full professors, while the non-full-professor tenured faculty members exist entirely in other departments.

In abstract terms, the structure of this flawed argument is:

  • All A are B.
  • Some B are not C.
  • Therefore, some A are not C.

Our goal is to find an answer choice that mirrors this exact invalid argument structure.
explanation_A:
Incorrect.

This argument can be structured as follows:

  • All modern office towers (M) are climate-controlled (C).
  • Some office buildings (O) are not climate-controlled (~C).
  • Therefore, some office buildings are not modern office towers (~M).

This is a valid argument. Since all modern office towers are climate-controlled, any office building that is not climate-controlled cannot possibly be a modern office tower. Since the argument is valid, it does not parallel the flawed reasoning of the stimulus.
explanation_B:
Incorrect.

This argument can be structured as:

  • All municipal hospital buildings (H) are massive (M).
  • Some municipal hospital buildings (H) are not forbidding (~F).
  • Therefore, some massive buildings (M) are not forbidding (~F).

This is a valid argument. Since the hospital buildings that are not forbidding must also be massive, we can guarantee that there is an overlap between massive buildings and non-forbidding buildings. Because this argument is logically valid, it does not parallel the flawed stimulus.
explanation_C:
Correct.

This argument is structured as:

  • All government buildings (G) are designed by famous architects (F).
  • Some buildings designed by famous architects (F) are not well proportioned (~P).
  • Therefore, some government buildings (G) are not well proportioned (~P).

This perfectly matches the flawed structure of the stimulus. Just because some buildings designed by famous architects are not well proportioned, it doesn't mean this must be true of any government buildings, even though all government buildings are designed by famous architects. The poorly proportioned buildings could all be non-government buildings. Thus, this is the same invalid argument form.
explanation_D:
Incorrect.

This argument attempts to draw a universal conclusion ("all poorly designed public buildings") from premises that only establish "some." While this is indeed a flaw, it does not parallel the specific quantifier-overlap flaw of the stimulus.
explanation_E:
Incorrect.

This argument can be structured as:

  • Some cathedrals (C) are not built of stone (~S).
  • All cathedrals (C) are impressive (I).
  • Therefore, some impressive buildings (I) are not built of stone (~S).

This is a valid argument. The cathedrals that are not built of stone are also impressive, which proves that some impressive buildings are not built of stone. Because the argument is valid, it cannot be the correct answer.

Explanation:
The argument attempts to establish that the chances of intelligent life emerging on a planet in any given planetary system are low. To support this, it relies on an analogy to Earth: Earth required large planets (Jupiter and Saturn) to protect it from frequent comet strikes, which would have prevented the rise of intelligent life. Since large planets are rare in other planetary systems, the author concludes that intelligent life must also be rare.

The core flaw in this argument is a causal/analogy assumption: it assumes that other planetary systems have the same threat of large comets as our solar system did. If other planetary systems do not contain many comets, then they do not need large planets to shield their habitable planets, and intelligent life could easily emerge there. Therefore, evaluating the threat of comets in other planetary systems is crucial to evaluating the validity of the argument.
explanation_A: A is incorrect. The total amount of matter from which a planetary system forms is not discussed in the argument and has no bearing on whether comets are present or whether large planets are necessary to shield life-supporting planets from them.
explanation_B: B is incorrect. This choice presents a common trap by confusing the survival of an existing intelligent species with the emergence (or arising) of intelligent life in the first place. The argument is specifically concerned with whether intelligent life will ever emerge on a planet, not how it would cope with a comet strike after already existing.
explanation_C: C is incorrect. The premise states that planetary systems are unlikely to contain any large planets. Whether a system needs one or two large planets to deflect comets is irrelevant if most systems are likely to have zero large planets.
explanation_D: D is correct. This choice directly addresses the crucial assumption in the argument. If the chances are high that other systems contain many comets, then the threat is real, and the lack of large shielding planets indeed makes the emergence of intelligent life unlikely (strengthening the argument). If the chances of containing many comets are very low, then there is no threat of frequent comet strikes, meaning planetary systems do not need large planets to develop intelligent life (weakening the argument).
explanation_E: E is incorrect. The argument already establishes in its opening premise that "the chances that a planet capable of supporting life will be formed are high." Knowing whether these habitable planets are specifically the size of Earth is not relevant to the argument's logic, which focuses on the relationship between life-supporting planets, comets, and protective large planets.

Explanation:
This is a Resolve-the-Paradox question. First, let's understand the two types of cost-plus contracts described in the stimulus:

  • Type 1 (Fixed Percentage of Cost): The contractor's profit is a fixed percentage of their costs (e.g., 10% of total costs). This means higher costs yield higher profits, giving the contractor an incentive to spend more.
  • Type 2 (Fixed Profit / "Fixed-Profit Kind"): The contractor's profit is a set, fixed amount over and above costs (e.g., $150 regardless of total costs). Under this contract, the contractor's profit does not change regardless of the final cost of the project.

The paradox is that, although contractors under Type 1 have an obvious incentive to run up costs to make more profit, cost overruns (final costs exceeding original estimates) are actually more common under Type 2 contracts.

To resolve this paradox, we need an answer choice that explains why costs are kept in check under Type 1, or why they are allowed to spiral out of control under Type 2.
explanation_A: This option introduces irrelevant details about the likelihood of projects being "scuttled" (canceled) under certain conditions. It does not explain why cost overruns are more common in one type of contract over the other.
explanation_B: This option explains why original cost projections might be underestimated in general (due to government-provided figures), but since this applies to all cost-plus contracts, it fails to explain the difference in cost overruns between Type 1 and Type 2 contracts.
explanation_C: This option states that clients can detect cost overruns early because they are billed periodically. However, because this applies to "any sizable construction project" under either type of contract, it does not distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 to explain the paradox.
explanation_D: Correct. This choice provides the necessary distinction that resolves the paradox. It states that clients only review billings to uncover wasteful expenditures when the contractor's profit varies with cost (which only happens under Type 1 contracts). Because clients actively monitor and police expenditures under Type 1 contracts, there is a strong downward pressure on costs. Under Type 2 contracts (fixed-profit), the contractor's profit does not vary with cost, so clients do not monitor billings as closely, leading to more frequent cost overruns.
explanation_E: This option suggests that under fixed-profit contracts (Type 2), contractors deliberately submit exaggeratedly high original cost estimates. If the original estimate is already exaggerated (very high), it should be much harder for final costs to exceed that estimate. Therefore, this option would make cost overruns less likely under Type 2, which deepens the paradox instead of resolving it.

Explanation:
This is a Resolve the Paradox question. The paradox is that we expect cost overruns (final costs exceeding original estimates) to be more common under percentage-of-cost contracts because contractors are incentivized to increase costs to boost their profits. However, cost overruns are actually more common under fixed-profit contracts.

We need an answer choice that explains this difference. If percentage-of-cost contracts are subject to some form of control or oversight that prevents overruns, or if fixed-profit contracts are somehow more prone to overruns despite the lack of direct incentive, that would resolve the paradox.
explanation_A: Incorrect. This choice discusses client willingness to agree to fixed-profit contracts depending on whether the project might be scuttled. However, client agreement has no clear impact on whether actual costs will exceed estimated costs once a contract is underway. Thus, it fails to explain the discrepancy in cost overruns between the two contract types.
explanation_B: Incorrect. This choice suggests that government inflation figures lead to underestimated projections. However, this underestimation would apply equally to both percentage-of-cost and fixed-profit contracts on long-term projects, so it does not explain why one type of contract has more overruns than the other.
explanation_C: Incorrect. This choice states that on any sizable project, billing is frequent enough to detect overruns early. Because this applies to both types of contracts on any sizable project, it does not differentiate between percentage-of-cost and fixed-profit contracts to explain why overruns are more common in the latter.
explanation_D: Correct. This choice explains that clients only review individual billings to uncover wasteful expenditures when the contractor's profit varies with cost (which occurs in percentage-of-cost contracts). Because clients of percentage-of-cost contracts closely monitor and police the expenditures, contractors are kept in check, resulting in fewer cost overruns. Under fixed-profit contracts, clients do not review the billings closely, allowing costs to rise unchecked and leading to more frequent cost overruns. This successfully resolves the paradox.
explanation_E: Incorrect. This choice states that contractors under fixed-profit contracts are more likely to submit exaggerated (inflated) initial cost estimates. If the initial cost estimates are deliberately exaggerated, final costs would be less likely to exceed those inflated estimates, meaning we would expect fewer cost overruns, not more. This choice actually makes the paradox harder to explain rather than resolving it.

Explanation:
Sasha argues that handwriting analysis should be banned in court because analysts habitually exaggerate the reliability of their analyses. Gregory agrees that the current use of handwriting analysis is indeed problematic. However, instead of banning it entirely, Gregory proposes a solution: establishing a licensing board to set professional standards. This would ensure that only licensed practitioners perform handwriting analysis, making it a legitimate courtroom tool.

Gregory's strategy is to defend the underlying legitimacy of handwriting analysis (the principle) by limiting its application to qualified, licensed professionals (restricting the class to which it is applied). This directly aligns with the description in choice (B).
explanation_A: This choice is incorrect because Gregory does not ignore Sasha's evidence. In fact, he explicitly concedes and agrees with her premise, stating, "You are right that the current use of handwriting analysis as evidence is problematic."
explanation_B: This is the correct answer. Gregory defends the principle that handwriting analysis can be a legitimate courtroom tool for character assessment by restricting its application to a specific, regulated class of people—namely, licensed practitioners rather than any self-proclaimed analyst.
explanation_C: This choice is incorrect because Gregory does not introduce specific evidence to abstract a general principle from it. He speaks in general terms about licensing boards and professional standards.
explanation_D: This choice is incorrect because Sasha's argument contains no self-contradictory statements, and Gregory does not attempt to find any logical contradiction in her words.
explanation_E: This choice is incorrect because Gregory does not suggest that Sasha's argument itself exhibits the undesirable characteristic (habitual exaggeration) that she condemns.

Explanation:
The question asks for a statement that, if true, would provide Sasha with the strongest counter to Gregory's response (i.e., weaken Gregory's argument).

Sasha argues that handwriting analysis should be banned in court because analysts habitually exaggerate the reliability of their analyses. Gregory agrees that the current practice is problematic but attributes this entirely to the lack of a licensing board. He claims that once a licensing board is established to set professional standards, handwriting analysis by licensed practitioners will become a legitimate courtroom tool.

Gregory's argument relies on a crucial assumption: that it is possible to be a responsible, professional handwriting analyst who legitimately claims that handwriting analysis provides reliable evidence of character. If no such person exists, then a licensing board cannot succeed in producing licensed practitioners who can provide legitimate character assessments.
explanation_A: This option is incorrect because the availability of other methods for character assessment does not undermine Gregory's claim that handwriting analysis can be made into a legitimate tool through licensing. The existence of alternative methods is irrelevant to whether this specific method can be improved and used.
explanation_B: This option actually supports the idea that highly trained professionals are needed, which aligns with Gregory's suggestion of a licensing board to establish standards and training. It does not weaken Gregory's argument.
explanation_C: This option suggests that some responsible analysts might be unfairly denied licenses. While this indicates that the licensing system might not be perfectly fair, it does not prevent the board from successfully licensing other responsible practitioners to make the field legitimate. It does not undermine the core of Gregory's solution.
explanation_D: This is the correct answer. If the only analysts who claim that handwriting provides reliable evidence of character are irresponsible, then any responsible analyst (the only ones who would be licensed under professional standards) must acknowledge that handwriting analysis does not provide reliable evidence of character. Consequently, a licensing board would either have to license no one (since anyone claiming it is reliable is irresponsible and thus fails the standards) or license people who admit the tool is unreliable, rendering it useless in court. This completely demolishes Gregory's proposed solution.
explanation_E: This option suggests that the number of analysts who could conform to the standards is very small. However, even if the pool of licensed practitioners is small, Gregory's plan of having a legitimate, albeit small, group of licensed practitioners still works. A small number of legitimate practitioners does not mean the tool itself cannot be legitimate.

Explanation: The argument in the stimulus follows a valid deductive form (Modus Ponens): if A, then B; A is true; therefore, B is true. Specifically, the conditional premise is: "The only thing that can have caused the bulge... is a broken joist" (Bulge → Broken Joist). Crucially, the premise also triggers the sufficient condition by referencing "the bulge that the wall now has" (the wall has a bulge). The conclusion is: "Therefore, at least one of the joists is broken." We need to find an argument that shares this structure: a conditional premise (X → Y) that simultaneously asserts that X has occurred, leading to an unconditional conclusion that Y is true.
explanation_A: This choice is a perfect match. The premise states: "nothing else would have made the conductor grimace..." (Grimace → Mistake). It triggers the sufficient condition with the phrase "in the way she just did," confirming she did grimace. The conclusion is: "At least one of the players... must have made a mistake." This mirrors the Modus Ponens structure of the stimulus precisely.
explanation_B: This choice is incorrect because the conclusion ("The first piece must have been the easiest") is an explanatory hypothesis for a phenomenon, rather than a deduction from a conditional rule. This represents causal/explanatory reasoning rather than conditional logic.
explanation_C: This choice is incorrect because its conclusion is a conditional statement ("The players play well only when they like the music"). The stimulus, however, concludes with an unconditional, absolute claim ("Therefore, at least one of the joists is broken").
explanation_D: This choice is incorrect because the premise contains a weak prescription ("specified that a harp should be played") rather than a strong, absolute conditional requirement. It does not match the deductive certainty of the stimulus.
explanation_E: This choice is incorrect because it is designed to explain a surprising situation (reconciling the conductor's anger with the orchestra's perfect playing) rather than establishing a standard Modus Ponens conditional deduction.

Explanation:
Sasha argues that handwriting analysis should be banned in court because analysts habitually exaggerate the reliability of their analyses. Gregory counters by claiming that this issue is solely due to the lack of a licensing board to set professional standards. He asserts that once such a board is established, handwriting analysis by licensed practitioners will become a legitimate courtroom tool. To weaken Gregory's argument, we need to find an option that shows a licensing board will not succeed in making handwriting analysis a legitimate courtroom tool.

Answer choice D achieves this by pointing out that any analyst who claims handwriting analysis can reliably assess character is inherently irresponsible. If this is true, a licensing board would either have to license irresponsible analysts (failing to solve the problem of exaggeration) or license only responsible ones (who would then admit the method is unreliable, making it useless in court). Thus, Gregory's solution of establishing a licensing board is rendered ineffective, providing Sasha with a powerful counterargument.
explanation_A: This choice states that courts have other ways to evaluate a person's character. However, the existence of alternative methods does not impact whether handwriting analysis itself can become a legitimate courtroom tool through the introduction of a licensing board. Therefore, it does not weaken Gregory's argument.
explanation_B: This choice points out a difficulty in handwriting analysis—that a single person can write in highly different styles. While this suggests the task is challenging and requires highly trained professionals, it does not undermine Gregory's assertion that a licensing board can successfully establish professional standards to ensure legitimacy.
explanation_C: This choice suggests that some responsible analysts might be denied licenses for reasons unrelated to their reliability. Even if the board unfairly excludes some qualified individuals, it does not prevent the licensed individuals from being legitimate and reliable practitioners. Thus, it does not weaken Gregory's conclusion.
explanation_D: This is the correct answer because it attacks a core assumption of Gregory's argument: that there can be responsible, licensed practitioners who provide reliable handwriting analyses of character. If the only analysts who claim handwriting analysis is reliable are irresponsible, then a licensing board cannot produce a pool of responsible practitioners who will testify to its reliability. The board would either have to certify irresponsible analysts or certify responsible ones who will testify that the method is unreliable, neither of which results in a legitimate courtroom tool.
explanation_E: This choice states that only a small number of analysts could meet the professional standards. Gregory's argument does not depend on having a large number of licensed practitioners; even a small group of legitimate experts would suffice to make handwriting analysis a viable courtroom tool. Therefore, this does not weaken his argument.

Explanation:
This question asks us to identify the flaw in the representative's counterargument. The core conflict in the passage centers on when the insurance policy became effective versus when the flight attendant died, due to a discrepancy between different time zones.

Instead of addressing this central contractual and chronological issue (i.e., whether 10 A.M. local time translates to before or after the policy's effective time of 9 A.M. in the purchase time zone), the flight attendant's representative argues that the policy should be paid because the flight attendant was his mother's sole support and she was ill. This argument relies entirely on invoking sympathy and pity rather than offering a logically relevant defense regarding the terms of the contract. Therefore, the argument is flawed because it makes an emotional appeal instead of addressing the substance of the dispute.
explanation_A: Option A: Incorrect. This option describes circular reasoning (where the premise simply restates the conclusion). Here, the premise (the mother is ill and needs support) is completely different from the conclusion (the insurance company should pay), so the argument is not circular.
explanation_B: Option B: Correct. This option accurately identifies the flaw. The representative attempts to win the dispute by appealing to emotions of pity (the mother's illness and financial dependency) rather than resolving the technical and legal question of when the policy actually went into effect.
explanation_C: Option C: Incorrect. The representative does not make or rely on a distinction between family obligations and business obligations. If anything, the representative is inappropriately conflating or mixing these two concepts by suggesting that family needs should dictate business/contractual payouts, rather than distinguishing them.
explanation_D: Option D: Incorrect. This option describes an ad hominem flaw, where an opponent's character is attacked instead of their argument. The representative does not attack the character of the insurance company or its agents.
explanation_E: Option E: Incorrect. This option describes a causal flaw (confusing cause and effect). There is no causal claim being made in the representative's argument, so this flaw is not present.

Explanation:
The stimulus describes a situation where a child's newly developed imagination (a cognitive capacity) first causes a problem: the creation of imaginary creatures that torment the child. However, this same capacity can also be used to solve the problem by allowing the child to imagine a toy as a powerful ally that wards off these threats.

This structure perfectly illustrates a situation where the source or cause of a problem also provides the means to resolve it. Therefore, the principle that most closely conforms to this scenario is that the cause of a problem can sometimes offer its solution.
explanation_A: Option (A) is incorrect because the stimulus explicitly states that the newly developed cognitive capacity (imagination) can be used to make the creatures harmless. Thus, it does not only give rise to problems.
explanation_B: Option (B) is the correct answer. The child's imagination is the cause of the problem (creating tormenting imaginary creatures), but it also provides the solution (creating an imaginary ally to ward off those creatures).
explanation_C: Option (C) is incorrect because the stimulus does not discuss whether children are capable of distinguishing between real and imaginary threats. It only describes how they use their imagination to deal with imaginary threats.
explanation_D: Option (D) is incorrect because the stimulus does not claim that acknowledging fears is the most effective way to address them. This is an extreme comparison not supported by the passage.
explanation_E: Option (E) is incorrect because it is far too broad. The passage focuses on children's imaginary fears and does not make general claims about 'most problems associated with child-rearing' or how parents should solve them.

Explanation: This is a Point of Disagreement question. We need to identify the claim about which Trisha and Jerod have opposing views. Trisha argues that today's family is declining and unable to perform its functions, suggesting a need to return to traditional values. This indicates she believes the contemporary family is not adequate as it is. Jerod, on the other hand, suggests leaving "what is good enough alone" and argues that contemporary criticisms are overblown, indicating he believes the family is adequate as it currently exists. Therefore, they disagree over whether the institution of the family is adequate as it is.
explanation_A: Correct. As discussed, Trisha believes that contemporary families are failing in child-rearing and stability, meaning they are not adequate as they are. Jerod believes contemporary families are "good enough" and should be left alone, meaning they are adequate as they are. This represents a clear point of disagreement.
explanation_B: Incorrect. Both speakers agree that the family is changing over time. Trisha notes that it is "declining" from its traditional state, and Jerod notes that contemporary families are "less stable than traditionally." Since they agree on this change, it cannot be the point of disagreement.
explanation_C: Incorrect. While Jerod mentions that "most people do not find [less stability] to be bad," Trisha does not express an opinion on what most people value or believe. We cannot establish a disagreement without knowing Trisha's view on this specific point.
explanation_D: Incorrect. Neither speaker discusses whether the institution of the family is going to survive. Trisha speaks of a decline and a need for reform, while Jerod speaks of its adequacy, but neither predicts its extinction.
explanation_E: Incorrect. Both speakers agree that the family is no longer traditional. Trisha calls for a "return to traditional values," implying they have been lost, and Jerod acknowledges that contemporary families differ from traditional ones. Because they agree on this, it is not the point of disagreement.

Explanation: The core of Politician P's argument is that because raising taxes would cause unhappiness among taxpayers (due to their loss of purchasing power), the opponent's claim that the government is obligated to raise taxes is false. This is a flawed line of reasoning because the negative consequences or unpopularity of an action do not necessarily mean that there is no moral or legal obligation to perform that action.
explanation_A: This choice describes a flaw where a claim is dismissed because the defender has other unpopular views. There is no mention of any other views held by the opponent, so this is incorrect.
explanation_B: This option describes a personal attack (ad hominem) on the opponent's character. Politician P does not attack the opponent's character, so this is incorrect.
explanation_C: This is the correct answer. The politician concludes that the opponent's view is false ("simply mistaken") on the grounds that implementing the policy would lead to unhappiness ("make taxpayers upset").
explanation_D: The issues raised (taxpayer unhappiness and loss of buying power) are not wholly irrelevant to the discussion of tax policy. Furthermore, the politician is not attempting to deflect attention, but rather to argue directly against the policy based on these negative outcomes.
explanation_E: This choice mischaracterizes the politician's conclusion. The politician is arguing that an obligation does not exist, rather than insisting that one does exist.

Explanation:
The question asks us to find the option that most seriously undermines the defense offered by the dean. The dean is defending the Hyperion School of Journalism against charges that its program is of little or no value. To do so, the dean points to a statistic: 65 percent of its graduates went on to internships or jobs in print or broadcast journalism. This is intended to show that the school successfully places its students into the industry, which implies the school's program is valuable.

To weaken this argument, we want to show that this 65 percent statistic does not necessarily demonstrate that the school added value. If the students already had journalism jobs or experience before coming to the school, the school cannot take credit for "placing" them in these roles. This would mean the program may still be of little or no value in terms of helping students secure employment.
explanation_A: Correct. This choice states that more than half of the students already came from jobs in journalism to improve their skills. If a large portion of the student body was already employed in journalism prior to entering the program, the fact that 65% of graduates ended up with journalism jobs or internships does not prove that the school's program helped them secure those positions. This heavily undermines the dean's claim that the placement statistic is a measure of the program's success and value.
explanation_B: This choice is incorrect because what "some" newspaper editors believe about journalism schools in general does not undermine the specific success or value of the Hyperion program. Furthermore, "some" is a very weak quantifier that could mean as few as two editors.
explanation_C: This choice is incorrect because a decline in the number of cities with multiple major newspapers over the last 25 years is an industry-wide trend that does not directly address the value of the Hyperion program or the validity of the dean's placement statistics.
explanation_D: This choice is incorrect because showing that Hyperion's program is similar in quality and content to peer institutions does not undermine the dean's defense. If anything, it suggests the program is standard, which doesn't support the claim that it is of little or no value.
explanation_E: This choice is incorrect because the selectivity of the admissions process (the proportion of applicants admitted) does not tell us whether the actual curriculum and program provide value to those who are admitted and graduate.

Explanation:
The question asks why Politician P's reasoning is questionable. We first need to identify the structure of the argument. Politician P argues against their opponent's claim that the government is obligated to raise taxes to increase funding for schools and healthcare. Politician P's premise is that doing so would make taxpayers upset due to a loss of buying power. From this, Politician P concludes that the opponent is simply mistaken (i.e., the claim that the government is obligated is false).

This is a classic flaw of concluding that an action shouldn't be taken or that an obligation doesn't exist simply because its implementation would cause people to be upset or unhappy. This fails to address the actual merits of the opponent's claim about obligation.
explanation_A: Option A: This option describes an ad hominem attack where a claim is rejected because its advocate holds other unpopular views. Politician P does not mention any other views held by their opponent, so this does not describe the flaw in the argument.
explanation_B: Option B: This option describes a different kind of ad hominem attack where a claim is rejected based on the defender's questionable character. Politician P does not attack the opponent's character, so this is incorrect.
explanation_C: Option C: This is the correct answer. Politician P concludes that the opponent's view is mistaken (false) on the grounds that raising taxes would make taxpayers upset (which is a form of unhappiness). The argument assumes that because a policy leads to some unhappiness, there cannot be an obligation to implement it.
explanation_D: Option D: This option claims that the politician appeals to wholly irrelevant issues to deflect attention from the real issue. However, Politician P is not trying to deflect attention away from the opponent's claim; rather, P is directly addressing and attempting to refute it, albeit with a flawed premise. Additionally, how taxpayers feel is not necessarily "wholly irrelevant" to policy decisions, even if it is insufficient to disprove an obligation.
explanation_E: Option E: This option describes a flaw of insisting that an obligation exists without evidence. However, Politician P is doing the opposite: arguing that an obligation does not exist. Thus, this option mischaracterizes the argument's conclusion.

Explanation: This is a "Must Be True" question, which means we must find the option that is logically supported by the facts provided in the stimulus. The stimulus tells us that Mars has a massive volcano (27 km high, size of Romania). It then states that even if Earth had the same low gravity as Mars, a volcano of this size could not exist on Earth because Earth's crust is too thin to support even a fraction of its mass without buckling and sinking. Since Mars' crust does support this massive volcano, we can infer that Mars' crust must be thicker than Earth's crust, at least under this volcano.
explanation_A: The stimulus contains no information about erosion or how it affects the surfaces of Mars and Earth. Thus, we cannot determine whether Mars is less subject to erosion than Earth.
explanation_B: While we know that a certain thickness of crust is necessary to support a massive volcano, the stimulus does not establish a direct correlation where the highest volcanoes must always occur where the crust is at its absolute thickest. Other factors might determine where volcanoes form and how high they grow.
explanation_C: We only know about the single largest volcano on Mars. We do not have any statistical data to compare the average height of all volcanoes on Mars to those on Earth.
explanation_D: Since Earth's crust is too thin to support the weight of Mars' largest volcano (even under Mars-like low gravity), and Mars' crust successfully supports it, Mars' crust must be thicker than Earth's crust at least at the location of this volcano.
explanation_E: This is a hypothetical claim that cannot be proven. Even if Earth had a thicker crust that was capable of supporting larger volcanoes, we cannot assume that volcanoes would actually grow larger, as there could be other constraints (such as volcanic activity levels or magma supply) keeping them at their current sizes.

Explanation:
The question asks us to identify the option that most seriously undermines the dean's defense of the Hyperion School of Journalism. The dean defends the school against charges that its program is of little or no value by pointing to a key statistic: 65 percent of its graduates went on to internships or jobs in print or broadcast journalism.

To weaken this argument, we need to show that this placement statistic does not actually demonstrate that the program provides significant value to its students. The dean assumes that the school's program is responsible for the graduates obtaining these positions.
explanation_A: Correct. This choice states that more than half of the school's students already had jobs in journalism before entering the program to improve their skills. If over 50% of the students already had journalism jobs, the 65% post-graduation placement rate is much less impressive and doesn't show that the school is successfully placing students who didn't already have career paths in journalism. Thus, it weakens the connection between the statistic and the dean's conclusion that the program provides substantial value in terms of placement.
explanation_B: Incorrect. Whether some newspaper editors view journalism school as a "necessary" part of training does not mean the school has no value. A program can be highly valuable even if it is not strictly necessary. Furthermore, this option does not address or explain away the dean's placement statistic.
explanation_C: Incorrect. A decline in the number of cities with multiple major newspapers is a general industry trend. It does not affect the validity of the dean's specific argument, which relies on the school's actual 65% placement rate to prove its value.
explanation_D: Incorrect. Pointing out that the program is similar in quality and content to peer institutions does not weaken the dean's argument because we do not know whether those peer programs are considered valuable or of little value. It lacks any direct impact on the usefulness of the 65% placement statistic.
explanation_E: Incorrect. The admissions rate (whether the school has become more selective over the last ten years) has no logical connection to whether the program provides value to those who graduate from it, nor does it address the placement rate.

Explanation:
The argument concludes that the recommendation to grant Caronian-speakers autonomy as an independent nation (where they constitute a majority) cannot be satisfied. The basis for this conclusion is that they live in widely scattered areas that cannot be enclosed within a single continuous boundary while still maintaining a Caronian majority. <\/p>

To connect the premise to the conclusion, the author must assume that a nation cannot consist of multiple disconnected, non-contiguous territories. If a nation could indeed be formed from disconnected regions, the scattered Caronian communities could be grouped together into a single nation of separate parts, thereby satisfying the recommendation. Thus, assuming that disconnected regions cannot satisfy the recommendation is necessary for the argument to hold.<\/p>
explanation_A: This option is incorrect because the past existence of a Caronian-majority nation has no bearing on whether the current recommendation can be practically satisfied under the existing geographical constraints.<\/p>
explanation_B: This option is incorrect because how Caronian-speakers perceive themselves does not affect the physical or political feasibility of establishing an autonomous nation under the given constraints.<\/p>
explanation_C: This option is correct. If we negate this statement to say that the recommendation could<\/em> be satisfied by a nation formed of disconnected regions, then the author's objection (that they cannot be united within a single continuous boundary) no longer prevents the recommendation from being satisfied. This negation collapses the argument, proving that the assumption is necessary.<\/p>
explanation_D: This option is incorrect because the recommendation only requires Caronian-speakers to form a majority<\/em> of the population, not the entirety of it. Therefore, it is not necessary to assume that no non-Caronian speakers will be included as citizens.<\/p>
explanation_E: This option is incorrect because whether multiple languages are spoken in most other nations is completely irrelevant to the specific geographical and demographic challenges of establishing a Caronian nation.<\/p>

Explanation: The question asks us to identify the main conclusion of the sociologist's argument. To find the main conclusion, we can analyze the structure of the argument. The first sentence states: "The welfare state cannot be successfully implemented because it rests on the assumption that human beings are unselfish—a seemingly false assumption." The word "because" introduces premises that support the claim preceding it. Therefore, the claim that the welfare state cannot be successfully implemented is supported by the subsequent statements, making it the main conclusion of the argument.
explanation_A: Correct. This choice accurately paraphrases the main conclusion of the argument, which is that "the welfare state cannot be successfully implemented." Saying "the welfare state will not work" is a direct and accurate simplified version of this main point.
explanation_B: Incorrect. While the argument describes how the welfare state requires wage earners to give up their funds to help others in need, it does not make a moral claim about fairness. Even if it did, this would be part of the premise structure explaining how the welfare state functions, rather than the main conclusion.
explanation_C: Incorrect. This statement represents an intermediate conclusion (or sub-conclusion) in the argument. The author argues that the assumption of human unselfishness is false in order to support the main conclusion that the welfare state cannot be successfully implemented. Therefore, it is a premise for the main conclusion, not the main conclusion itself.
explanation_D: Incorrect. This option is a minor premise that supports the idea that people innately seek their own well-being. It serves to establish that humans are generally selfish, which in turn supports the main conclusion, but it is not the main conclusion of the argument.
explanation_E: Incorrect. This is a premise used to establish why the welfare state relies on an unselfish attitude. It supports the claim that the welfare state relies on a false assumption, which ultimately supports the main conclusion, but is not the main conclusion itself.

Explanation:
This is a Most Strongly Supported question. Let's analyze the information provided in the stimulus:

  • Early pencil leads were made of solid graphite mined in Cumberland, Britain.
  • Modern methods of manufacturing pencil leads from powdered graphite resulted from research sponsored by the French government in the 1790s.
  • During the 1790s, France was at war with Britain and had no access to Cumberland graphite.

From these facts, we can infer a need-based motivation: France lost access to their source of solid graphite (Cumberland) and was forced to research a new method using powdered graphite. This strongly suggests that they did not have access to any other source of solid graphite that could meet their pencil needs at the time; otherwise, they would have likely just used that alternative source instead of inventing an entirely new manufacturing process.
explanation_A: This choice is too strong and unsupported. The stimulus only tells us that early pencils used graphite from Cumberland, not that Cumberland was the only deposit of suitable graphite in the entire world. There could have been other undiscovered or unused deposits elsewhere.
explanation_B: Correct. This is strongly supported by the stimulus. If the French government had known of and had access to another source of solid graphite suitable for making pencils, they would not have needed to sponsor research to develop a brand new technology to manufacture pencils from powdered graphite. The fact that they funded this research because they lost access to Cumberland's solid graphite indicates they had no other accessible source of solid graphite.
explanation_C: This choice introduces an unsupported causal claim. While we are told that France and Britain were at war, the stimulus does not suggest that the war was caused by disputes over graphite exports or pencils.
explanation_D: This choice makes a broad generalization ("frequently") about government-sponsored research. A single historical instance of government-funded research yielding a beneficial invention (powdered graphite pencils) is not enough to support a claim about what "frequently" happens.
explanation_E: This choice is unsupported. The stimulus states that modern methods of manufacturing pencil leads from powdered graphite were developed as an alternative to using Cumberland's solid graphite. There is no reason to believe that all modern pencils contain Cumberland graphite today.

Explanation: The argument concludes that passengers are safer on airplanes equipped with a collision-avoidance radar system than on planes without it, despite the concession that the system frequently triggers false alarms (warning pilots to evade "phantom" airplanes). The weakness in the argument lies in this concession: if the system frequently causes pilots to take unnecessary evasive actions, and if those evasive actions themselves pose a risk to passenger safety, then the system might actually make flying less safe. To strengthen the argument, we need to show that these evasive maneuvers are not dangerous.
explanation_A: Correct. This choice directly addresses the main vulnerability in the argument. If evasive action taken in response to the system's warnings poses no risk to the passengers, then the frequent false alarms (evading "phantom" airplanes) do not compromise safety. This removes a major objection to the system and strongly supports the conclusion that equipped planes are safer.
explanation_B: This choice states that planes are in greater danger of colliding on the ground than in flight. This is irrelevant to whether the collision-avoidance radar system makes planes safer while in flight. Comparing ground safety to flight safety does not help us evaluate the utility of this in-flight system.
explanation_C: This choice tells us that mid-air collisions are rare. While this is reassuring, it does not tell us whether planes with the radar system are safer than those without it. Even if collisions are rare, having the system could still make passengers relatively safer, or the frequent false alarms could still make it less safe.
explanation_D: This choice states that 63 percent of the warnings were invalid. This actually highlights and quantifies the weakness in the system (the false alarms), which, if anything, tends to weaken the argument rather than strengthen it, especially without knowing if those invalid warnings lead to dangerous maneuvers.
explanation_E: This choice provides technical details about how the system works (computerized, scans the sky, calculates distances). While informative, these details do not address the safety impact of the false alarms or help establish that equipped planes are safer than unequipped ones.

Explanation:
This is a Necessary Assumption question. The argument concludes that passengers are safer on airplanes equipped with a collision-avoidance radar system than on airplanes without it, despite the fact that the system frequently gives false alarms (warning of 'phantom airplanes').

For the system to actually make passengers safer, the pilots must actually respond to the system's warnings. If the frequent false alarms caused pilots to routinely disregard the warnings, the system would fail to provide any safety benefit. Therefore, the argument depends on the assumption that these false alarms do not lead pilots to ignore the system.
explanation_A: This choice addresses how passengers feel about their safety. The conclusion of the argument is about whether they actually are safer, which is an objective measure. Subjective feelings of safety are irrelevant to the logical validity of the argument.
explanation_B: The underlying cause of the false alarms (whether they are caused by distorted radar signals or something else) does not affect the argument. Regardless of what causes them, the key issue is how pilots respond to them.
explanation_C: This is the correct answer. If we negate this statement, it becomes: 'The frequency of invalid warnings will cause pilots routinely to disregard the system's warnings.' If pilots routinely disregard the warnings, the system cannot make the passengers safer, which completely undermines the author's conclusion.
explanation_D: Whether other types of planes can use this system is completely outside the scope of the argument, which is strictly concerned with the safety of passengers on commercial passenger airplanes.
explanation_E: This is a common trap choice. The system does not need to address the greatest safety risk in order to make passengers safer. Even if midair collisions are a relatively minor risk compared to other hazards, preventing them still results in a net increase in passenger safety.

Explanation: This is a Necessary Assumption question. We are asked to find the option that is absolutely required for the television station's plan to achieve its stated purpose, which is to "forewarn parents about the level of violence in any given program." The plan relies on child psychologists rating the programs and listing those ratings (represented by one to four guns) in the newspapers.
explanation_A: Correct. This is a necessary assumption for the plan to work. If parents do not read or pay attention to the ratings listed in the newspapers, then placing those ratings in the newspapers will fail to forewarn them. Negating this choice ("Parents would not read and pay attention to the ratings...") completely destroys the argument, proving that it is a necessary assumption.
explanation_B: This is incorrect. The relative number of highly violent shows compared to shows with low levels of violence is irrelevant to whether the rating system succeeds in forewarning parents.
explanation_C: This is incorrect. The system does not need to be the "most" effective system available for the plan to meet its purpose; it simply needs to be effective enough to forewarn parents.
explanation_D: This is incorrect. Whether the television station has a moral or legal obligation to forewarn parents is irrelevant to the practical question of whether this specific plan will succeed in forewarning them.
explanation_E: This is incorrect. The stated purpose of the plan is merely to forewarn parents about the violence levels, not to force television producers to reduce the violence. Therefore, we do not need to assume that producers will try to reduce violence levels.

Explanation: The argument transitions from a country-level correlation (average fat intake is correlated with cancer incidence) to an individual causal recommendation (individuals should reduce fat intake to reduce cancer risk). This relies on the classic assumption of correlation implying causation. To weaken such an argument, the most effective strategy is to introduce a confounding variable (an alternative cause) that could explain both elements of the correlation, showing that fat intake itself may not be the cause of the increased cancer risk.
explanation_A: This option explains why different countries have different fat intakes (due to traditional diets). However, this does not weaken the argument because it has no bearing on the relationship between fat intake and cancer.
explanation_B: This choice suggests that countries with high fat intake are among the wealthiest. While wealth is a correlating factor, it is not a plausible cause of cancer. Therefore, it does not successfully present an alternative cause for the cancer rates, unlike option (D).
explanation_C: This is a classic trap answer. Knowing that cancer is a "prominent cause of death" in countries with low average fat intake does not contradict the premise that the overall incidence of cancer is lower in those countries. It is entirely consistent with the premises and does not weaken the argument.
explanation_D: This is the correct answer. It introduces a highly plausible confounding variable: environmental pollution. Since countries with high average fat intake also have the highest levels of pollution, it is possible that pollution (and not fat intake) is the true cause of the higher cancer rates. This seriously undermines the conclusion that individuals should reduce fat intake to lower their cancer risk.
explanation_E: This option states that an individual's diet may differ from their country's average. While this is a true statistical reality (avoiding the ecological fallacy), it does not address or weaken the causal link between fat intake and cancer risk asserted by the argument.

Explanation:
This is a Resolve/Explain question. We are asked to find the option that most helps explain the puzzling fact presented in the stimulus: why do modern tree-dwelling kangaroos lack prehensile tails and opposable thumbs, even though their ancestors had them and they would be highly beneficial for their current lifestyle in trees?

The stimulus tells us that the common ancestors of both land-dwelling and tree-dwelling kangaroos possessed these traits. While it is expected that land-dwelling kangaroos lost them because they offer no advantage on land, it is highly surprising that modern tree-dwelling kangaroos also lack them. To resolve this paradox, we need an explanation for why the tree-dwelling species lost these traits.
explanation_A: This choice is incorrect because it deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it. If modern tree-dwelling kangaroos have difficulty descending trees because they lack opposable thumbs, it makes it even more mysterious why they would have lost such a useful attribute.
explanation_B: This choice is incorrect because size comparisons between different kangaroo species and their ancestors are irrelevant. Knowing their relative sizes does not help explain the loss of specific anatomical traits like prehensile tails and opposable thumbs.
explanation_C: This choice is incorrect because it merely describes the current physical attributes of modern tree-dwelling kangaroos' tails (longer and more flexible) without explaining why they lost the prehensile (grasping) ability.
explanation_D: This choice is correct because it explains the evolutionary lineage. If modern tree-dwelling kangaroos descended from land-dwelling ancestors that had already lost these traits over many generations on the ground, then the modern tree-dwelling kangaroos started their evolution without them and simply have not re-developed them yet.
explanation_E: This choice is incorrect because details about hind leg strength and movement speed on land do not explain the absence of tree-dwelling adaptations like grasping tails and opposable thumbs.

Explanation:
The editorialist’s argument relies on a shift in the meaning of a key term: "maturity."

First, the editorialist establishes a rule: society should grant the privileges of adulthood once members are "mature enough to accept the corresponding responsibilities." This type of maturity is psychological, cognitive, or moral.

Next, the editorialist introduces a scientific premise: "physiological development is completed in most persons by age seventeen." This refers to physical, biological maturity.

By concluding that seventeen-year-olds should be granted the privileges of adulthood because they have completed "this maturing process," the author treats biological maturity as equivalent to moral or psychological maturity. This logical flaw is known as equivocation.
explanation_A: Incorrect. This option describes circular reasoning (assuming what one is trying to prove). The author does not assume that seventeen-year-olds should get adult privileges; rather, they attempt to prove this claim by inappropriately linking physiological maturity to moral responsibility.
explanation_B: Incorrect. This option describes a hasty generalization based on an unrepresentative sample. The argument does not base its conclusion on a few select examples; instead, it references a broad scientific claim about "most persons."
explanation_C: Correct. This choice correctly identifies the flaw of equivocation. The argument shifts between two distinct meanings of "mature/maturing": cognitive/moral maturity (capable of handling responsibility) and physiological maturity (physical development).
explanation_D: Incorrect. The editorialist refers to what "science has established" regarding physiological development. Science is a highly appropriate authority on biological growth, so this is not an appeal to an inappropriate authority.
explanation_E: Incorrect. Whether some sixteen-year-olds are mature is irrelevant to the logical connection (or lack thereof) between the biological and moral maturity of seventeen-year-olds.

Explanation: The video analyzes a Parallel Reasoning question. It begins by identifying the logical structure of the stimulus: "Every new play that runs for more than three months (N3+) is either a commercial success (CM) or a critical success (CR)." This can be diagrammed as: $N3+ \rightarrow CM \lor CR$. Next, "Last year, all new plays that were critical successes were also commercial successes," which is $CR \rightarrow CM$. The conclusion is: "Therefore, last year every new play that ran for more than three months was a commercial success," or $N3+ \rightarrow CM$. This is a valid argument, as any $N3+$ play must be either $CM$ or $CR$. Since all $CR$ plays are also $CM$, any $N3+$ play is guaranteed to be a $CM$. We need to find an answer choice that mirrors this exact logical structure: $A \rightarrow B \lor C$, $C \rightarrow B$, therefore $A \rightarrow B$.
explanation_A: Answer choice (A) is incorrect because it uses the term "most" instead of "all" or "every." The stimulus relies on strict conditional statements (universal quantifiers), so an answer choice that relies on probability or majority ("most") cannot be a parallel match.
explanation_B: Answer choice (B) is incorrect because its first premise states that every best-selling cookbook is both well written and contains beautiful photographs, whereas the stimulus uses an either/or disjunction. Additionally, the argument commits a fallacy of the converse by concluding that Cynthia's cookbook must be a best-selling cookbook because it has both characteristics.
explanation_C: Answer choice (C) is the correct answer. It perfectly mirrors the logical structure of the stimulus. Let $A$ be second-year students at the Freeman School, $D$ be studying desserts, and $S$ be studying soups. The first premise states that all second-year students study either desserts or soups ($A \rightarrow D \lor S$). The second premise states that all students studying soups also study desserts ($S \rightarrow D$). The conclusion correctly infers that all second-year students study desserts ($A \rightarrow D$).
explanation_D: Answer choice (D) is incorrect because it uses an exclusive "either/or" ("but not both") and draws a conclusion about a specific individual (John Endicott) rather than a universal group. The stimulus concludes with a general conditional statement ("every new play...").
explanation_E: Answer choice (E) is incorrect because, like (B), it uses a conjunction ("both... and...") instead of a disjunction ("either... or..."). It also applies contrapositive reasoning to draw a conclusion about a specific business ("Peggy's Fine Foods"), which does not match the universal, non-negational structure of the stimulus's argument.

Explanation:
This is a "Flaw-Except" question, phrased as "LEAST vulnerable to which one of the following criticisms." Four of the answer choices will point out genuine flaws in the commissioner's reasoning, while the correct answer will describe a criticism that is either inaccurate or irrelevant to the argument's actual weaknesses.

The commissioner's argument defends their decision-making on a power plant issue. The commissioner admits to basing the decision entirely on a neighborhood association's report without studying it thoroughly, yet assumes it is accurate. Furthermore, they attempt to justify this reliance by pointing out that they agreed with the association's recommendation on a completely different issue (jail relocation) in the past. This reasoning is highly flawed in several ways: it relies on a potentially biased source, assumes a single report is sufficient, presumes accuracy without investigation, and incorrectly assumes past agreement on one issue guarantees the validity of another recommendation.
explanation_A: This is a valid criticism. A neighborhood association is highly likely to have a specific interest or bias regarding local developments like a power plant. By relying entirely on their report, the commissioner assumes without justification that the information is unbiased.
explanation_B: This is the correct answer. The commissioner's argument is least vulnerable to this criticism because there is no indication that the conclusion is based on "incomplete recollections." The commissioner recalls agreeing with a past recommendation, and there is no reason to doubt this memory or suggest it is incomplete. This choice describes a flaw that does not occur in the stimulus.
explanation_C: This is a valid criticism. The commissioner bases their entire decision on a single report from the neighborhood association, implicitly assuming that no other direct evidence or alternative perspectives need to be considered.
explanation_D: This is a valid criticism. The commissioner explicitly admits, "although I have not studied it thoroughly, I am sure that the information it contains is accurate." It is a clear flaw to deem a report accurate without actually investigating it in detail.
explanation_E: This is a valid criticism. The commissioner brings up a past instance regarding jail relocation to justify their current agreement on the power plant issue. This is a non-sequitur; agreeing with them in the past on an unrelated topic does not logically justify relying on their current report.

Explanation:
This is a Resolve the Paradox question. We are asked to explain why the order of the tasks did not affect the performance of beginning readers, who always performed better on the paragraph than on the list of words.

For experienced readers, the order mattered because they made fewer errors on the task they performed second, likely due to practice or familiarity. However, for beginning readers, they always performed better on the paragraph, regardless of whether they read it first or second. To resolve this, we need an explanation that shows why beginning readers are uniquely dependent on the format of the paragraph (which provides context) and why previous exposure to the words (order) doesn't help them when reading the list.
explanation_A: Choice A explains that the paragraph contains repeated words while the list does not. While this highlights a difference between the two tasks, it does not explain why the order of the tasks had no effect on the beginning readers. If anything, reading the paragraph first (with its repeated words) should have helped them recognize those words in the list later, which would make the order of tasks significant.
explanation_B: Choice B compares how experienced readers and beginning readers use context in the paragraph. However, this choice focuses on why experienced readers might be better, rather than explaining the specific performance pattern of the beginning readers (specifically, why order did not matter to them and why they always excelled on the paragraph).
explanation_C: Choice C is the correct answer. It states that beginning readers rely solely on context to guess difficult words. A paragraph provides context, whereas a randomly ordered list of words does not. This explains why beginning readers always did better on the paragraph (where context was available) than on the list (where it was not), regardless of which task they performed first. Since they cannot use context to help them read the list, having previously read the paragraph does not improve their performance on the list, explaining why the order of tasks was insignificant for them.
explanation_D: Choice D suggests that reading the words in the first task should help children recognize them in the second task. If this were true for beginning readers, then the order of the tasks would have had a significant effect on their performance, which directly contradicts the passage.
explanation_E: Choice E merely states that beginning readers made more errors overall than experienced readers. While this is likely true, it does not explain why the order of the tasks had no effect on the beginning readers or why they always performed better on the paragraph than on the list.

Explanation:
This is a Flaw-Except question, meaning the correct answer is the only option that does NOT describe a flaw in the commissioner's argument. The other four choices will be valid criticisms of the argument.

The commissioner argues that their decision on the power plant was not premature, relying on a report by the neighborhood association. However, the commissioner admits to not having studied the report thoroughly (though they are somehow sure it is accurate) and tries to justify this reliance by pointing out that they agreed with the association's recommendation on a past, unrelated issue (jail relocation).
explanation_A: This option describes a genuine flaw. By assuming that the report is accurate without studying it thoroughly, the commissioner is taking for granted that the information has not been distorted by bias.
explanation_B: This is the correct answer because it does not describe a flaw present in the argument. 'Incomplete recollections' refers to memory lapses or forgetting. The commissioner's issue is not that they are misremembering the report, but rather that they have not studied it thoroughly in the first place. Therefore, the argument is not vulnerable to this criticism.
explanation_C: This option describes a genuine flaw. By defending the decision as not premature solely because they looked at this single report, the commissioner assumes that no other direct evidence needed to be considered.
explanation_D: This option describes a genuine flaw. The commissioner explicitly admits to not studying the report thoroughly while simultaneously claiming to be sure that it is accurate, which is a textbook hasty conclusion.
explanation_E: This option describes a genuine flaw. The commissioner attempts to justify relying on the association's current report by noting that they agreed with the association's past recommendation on jail relocation. This assumes a past agreement on an unrelated issue is relevant to the current decision.

Explanation:
This is a Must Be True EXCEPT question. The task is to identify the one answer choice that cannot be logically inferred from the stimulus. The four incorrect answer choices can be logically inferred based on information provided by the anthropologist.

The anthropologist states that violence is an extreme form of aggression and is distinct from the self-expression needed for survival under normal conditions. Additionally, reacting with violence is purely a result of cultural conditioning.
explanation_A: This choice can be logically inferred. The stimulus describes violence as an "extreme form of aggression," which implies that there are other, less extreme forms of aggression that do not amount to violence. Therefore, not all aggression is violent.
explanation_B: This is the correct answer because it cannot be logically inferred. The stimulus states that violence is distinct from the self-expression sufficient for survival, which means this survival-related self-expression is nonviolent. However, we cannot conclude that it is "generally nonaggressive." It could still involve some nonviolent forms of aggression.
explanation_C: This choice can be logically inferred. The anthropologist states that human beings react with violence only because they are conditioned by their culture. Since violence is a behavior, it follows that some behaviors are influenced by culture.
explanation_D: This choice can be logically inferred. Since violence is distinct from the self-expression required for survival under normal conditions, it follows that in normal circumstances, humans can survive without resorting to violence (i.e., by responding nonviolently).
explanation_E: This choice can be logically inferred. The stimulus asserts that humans react with violence "only because they are conditioned by their culture to react in this manner," directly supporting the claim that violent behavior is a product of one's cultural environment.

Explanation:
This is an Inference EXCEPT question (also known as a Must Be True EXCEPT question). The four incorrect options can be logically inferred from the passage, while the correct option cannot be inferred. Let's break down the anthropologist's statements:

1. Violence is an extreme form of aggression. This suggests that aggression exists on a spectrum, with violence at the most extreme end. Thus, there are other, less extreme forms of aggression that are not violent.

2. Violence is distinct from the self-expression sufficient for survival under normal conditions.

3. Humans react with violence to unpleasant stimuli only because of cultural conditioning. This means culture is the sole cause of these violent reactions.
explanation_A: Incorrect. This statement can be logically inferred from the passage. Since violence is described as an "extreme form of aggression," it implies that other, less extreme forms of aggression exist that are not violent. Since this choice can be inferred, it is incorrect on an EXCEPT question.
explanation_B: Correct. This statement cannot be logically inferred for two main reasons. First, the stimulus discusses self-expression sufficient (enough) for survival, whereas this option mentions self-expression required (necessary) for survival; sufficiency and necessity are distinct. Second, even if we overlook that distinction, the passage only tells us that this self-expression is distinct from violence. It does not state that it is nonaggressive. It could very well involve nonviolent forms of aggression. Since this cannot be inferred, it is the correct answer.
explanation_C: Incorrect. This statement can be logically inferred. The passage explicitly states that humans react with violence in certain situations only because of cultural conditioning. Violence is a behavior, so some behaviors are indeed influenced by culture. Since this can be inferred, it is incorrect.
explanation_D: Incorrect. This statement can be logically inferred. The passage states that violence is distinct from the self-expression sufficient for survival under normal conditions (normal circumstances). Since this self-expression is sufficient for survival and does not include violence, human beings can survive in normal circumstances without resorting to violence (i.e., nonviolently). Since this can be inferred, it is incorrect.
explanation_E: Incorrect. This statement can be logically inferred. The final sentence of the stimulus establishes that when humans react to unpleasant stimuli with violence, they do so "only because they are conditioned by their culture." This directly supports the idea that this violent behavior is a product of one's cultural environment. Since this can be inferred, it is incorrect.

Explanation:
The attorney concludes that Ziegler must have been insane at the time of the shooting because the prosecution only provided evidence that he was sane after the shooting, claiming this means there is no evidence of his sanity at the time of the trigger pull.

The flaw is that the attorney fails to recognize that evidence of sanity shortly after an event is, in fact, circumstantial evidence of sanity during the event itself. Thus, the premise that there is 'no evidence' of sanity at the time of the shooting is false.
explanation_A: This option is incorrect because the argument does not address whether being a well-educated professional is relevant to guilt or innocence, nor does it make any assumptions regarding Ziegler's education level.
explanation_B: This option mischaracterizes the relationship between the premises and the conclusion. The argument doesn't conclude that there is a lack of evidence of sanity based on evidence against sanity; rather, it uses the alleged lack of evidence of sanity at the time of the shooting as a premise to conclude that Ziegler was insane.
explanation_C: This option is incorrect because Ziegler's sanity during his time working as a consultant is not the focus of the argument, nor does ignoring this possibility constitute the primary logical flaw.
explanation_D: This option is incorrect because the attorney's argument does not address or presume anything about moral responsibility. It only attempts to establish a claim of insanity.
explanation_E: This is the correct answer. The attorney claims there is no evidence of Ziegler's sanity at the time of the shooting because the only evidence provided of his sanity comes from after the shooting. This argument fails to recognize that sanity after the shooting can reasonably indicate sanity at the time of the shooting, meaning there is indeed some evidence of his sanity.

Explanation:
The question asks us to identify the option that exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to Martha's. Let's analyze the structure of Martha's argument: <\/p>

Martha's Premises:<\/strong>
1. There are daisies that are a kind of chrysanthemum (Some Daisies are Chrysanthemums).
2. There are edible chrysanthemums that are palatable (Some Chrysanthemums are Edible and Palatable).<\/p>

Martha's Conclusion:<\/strong>
Her friend's claim is incorrect, meaning there are daisies that are edible and palatable (Some Daisies are Edible and Palatable).<\/p>

The Flaw:<\/strong>
This is a classic overlapping groups flaw of the form: 'Some A are B' and 'Some B are C,' therefore 'Some A are C.' This is invalid because the chrysanthemums that are daisies do not necessarily overlap with the chrysanthemums that are edible and palatable. We need an answer choice that mirrors this exact invalid 'Some\/Some' structure.<\/p>
explanation_A: Option A is incorrect.<\/strong> This argument commits a division fallacy (part-to-whole \/ whole-to-part). It reasons that because the city chorus as a whole is renowned, a specific member (Jeanne) must be an excellent singer. This does not match the overlapping 'Some\/Some' flaw in the stimulus.<\/p>
explanation_B: Option B is incorrect.<\/strong> This is a valid deduction: Rolfe is in the group, and all members of the group are avid readers, so Rolfe must be an avid reader. Since it is a valid argument, it cannot represent the flawed reasoning of the stimulus.<\/p>
explanation_C:
Option C is the correct answer.<\/strong> This option perfectly mirrors the invalid 'Some\/Some' structure of the stimulus:<\/p>

Premises:<\/strong>
1. Some of Noriko's sisters are on the debate team (Some Sisters are Debate team members).
2. Some members of the debate team are poor students (Some Debate team members are Poor students).<\/p>

Conclusion:<\/strong>
At least one of Noriko's sisters is a poor student (Some Sisters are Poor students).<\/p>

Just like in the stimulus, this argument incorrectly assumes that two separate subgroups of a middle category (the debate team) must overlap.<\/p>
explanation_D: Option D is incorrect.<\/strong> This argument is logically valid. It states that 'Most of Leon's friends are good swimmers' and 'Good swimmers are quite strong.' Since all good swimmers are strong, any friend who is a good swimmer must also be strong. Since most of his friends are good swimmers, at least some of them must be strong. Since the reasoning is valid, it does not match the flawed reasoning of the stimulus.<\/p>
explanation_E: Option E is incorrect.<\/strong> This argument introduces a term shift (writing books on the topic of 'good writing' vs. actually being a 'good writer') and does not follow the 'Some A are B, Some B are C, therefore Some A are C' logical structure.<\/p>

Explanation:
This is an Assumption Except question. Four of the answer choices are necessary assumptions that the argument relies upon, while the correct answer choice is not a necessary assumption.

The argument begins with the premise that history courses usually bore students because they focus heavily on dates and statistics. It concludes that the best way to teach history is to spend most class time recounting the lives of historical figures and very little time on dates and statistics. This argument assumes that avoiding boredom is a desirable goal, that the proposed method is compatible with the goals of teaching history, and that students will indeed be less bored by recounting lives than by learning dates and statistics.
explanation_A: Option (A) is a necessary assumption. If avoiding boring students is not a goal or shouldn't be done, then the fact that current methods bore students wouldn't be a reason to change them to find a 'better' way. Thus, the argument relies on this assumption.
explanation_B: Option (B) is a necessary assumption. If spending very little time on dates and statistics was incompatible with the attainable goals of teaching history, then the proposed method could not be the 'best way' to teach history, as it would fail to achieve the subject's goals. Therefore, the argument depends on this assumption.
explanation_C: Option (C) is the correct answer because it is NOT a necessary assumption. The conclusion proposes spending 'very little' class time on dates and statistics, not 'no' time. Even if it is impossible to recount the lives of historical figures without referring to some dates and statistics, the proposed method could still be implemented as long as those references occupy very little class time. Therefore, the argument does not need to assume that it is possible to recount lives without any reference to dates and statistics.
explanation_D: Option (D) is a necessary assumption. Similar to (B), if spending most class time recounting the lives of historical figures was incompatible with the goals of teaching history, this method could not be considered the 'best way' to teach the subject. Thus, the argument depends on this assumption.
explanation_E: Option (E) is a necessary assumption. The argument's recommendation is based on solving the problem of student boredom. If students would be just as bored (or even more bored) by a class focused on recounting historical lives, then changing the curriculum would not solve the problem of boredom, and the proposed method would not be the 'best way'. Thus, the argument must assume that students will be less bored by the new method.

Explanation:
This is a Sufficient Assumption (Principle) question. We are asked to find a principle that, if valid, helps justify the judge's conclusion that the evidence was inadmissible.
